subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation and length of the common chord of the two circles x² + y² + 2x + 2y + 1 = 0, x² + y² + 4x + 3y + 2 = 0.

mark_split.label: Find the length of the chord

insider_note: The common chord IS the radical axis of the two circles — the same S − S′ = 0 line from the radical-centre questions, only now used as an actual chord with a length to compute.

steps.label: Find the common chord
steps.margin_note: First mark. Same subtraction as a radical axis — the common chord is that same line.
lines: Equation of the common chord is S − S′ = 0
steps.why: Where two circles genuinely intersect, S − S′ = 0 is the line through both points of intersection — the common chord itself, not merely a radical axis with no real chord.
common_mistakes: Stopping at −2x − y − 1 = 0 without multiplying by −1 to clear the leading minus sign.
Subtracting S′ − S instead of S − S′ and then using the wrong sign convention downstream.
steps.memory_tip: Common chord = S minus S′ = 0 — literally the same line as a radical axis; only the geometric picture (an actual chord, not just a line) is different.

steps.label: Find the centre and radius
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Either circle works — the perpendicular distance is measured from ONE of them.
lines: For the circle S ≡ x² + y² + 2x + 2y + 1 = 0
steps.why: The length of a chord is found from ONE circle's own centre and radius together with the perpendicular distance from that same centre to the chord.
common_mistakes: Reading the centre as (1, 1) instead of (−1, −1) — the centre is (−g, −f), the negative of half the coefficients.
Using S′'s centre in this step but S's radius later, mixing the two circles.
steps.memory_tip: Centre is the negative of half the x and y coefficients: g = 1, f = 1, so centre is (−1, −1).

steps.label: Find the perpendicular distance
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for the distance from the centre chosen in step 2 to the chord found in step 1.
lines: Length of the perpendicular from C(−1, −1)
steps.why: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord — its length p, together with the radius r, gives a right triangle whose other leg is half the chord.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong circle's centre in the distance formula after finding both centres in earlier working.
Dropping the absolute value and carrying a negative distance forward.
steps.memory_tip: p = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C| / √(A² + B²), with (x₁, y₁) the centre found in the previous step.

steps.label: Find the length of the chord
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark, for the final chord length.
steps.why: Half the chord, the perpendicular distance p, and the radius r form a right triangle — Pythagoras gives half the chord as √(r² − p²), and the full chord is twice that.
common_mistakes: Writing r² − p² the wrong way round as p² − r², which gives a negative number under the root.
Forgetting the factor of 2 and stopping at half the chord length.
steps.memory_tip: Chord length is always 2 × √(radius² − distance²) — the same formula used for any chord, not special to a common chord.
